regions.name: Somló
regions.summary: Somló is a single extinct volcano standing alone on the flat country of western Hungary, north-west of Lake Balaton, and it is the smallest wine district in the country. The hill is white wine almost entirely: Juhfark, the grape named for its sheep's-tail bunch, with Furmint, Hárslevelű and Olaszrizling beside it. The wines are lean and high in acid, smoky and saline rather than fruity, and they open slowly over years. The fame is old: the Habsburg court drank the hill's wine, and legend made it the wine of the wedding night. The protected name on a label is Somlói; the district's administrative name is Nagy-Somló.

terroir.climate: Continental, with a cold winter and a warm, dry summer, but the hill rises alone from flat land and is swept by wind on every side, which dries the bunches after rain and keeps rot in check. Nights are cool on the upper slopes, and the dark basalt holds the day's heat and gives it back after sunset. Ripening is slow, acidity stays high, and that acid is the first thing the wines show.
terroir.soils: A basalt cap sits over layers of basalt tuff and ash, and under those lie the sand and clay of the Pannonian inland sea that once filled the basin. On the slopes the soil is a thin, dark, stony weathering of the basalt; loess and sand gather at the foot. The volcanic ground is the reason the growers give for the smoke and flint in the glass.
terroir.topography: The hill is a butte, a flat-topped cone a little over four hundred metres high with a ring of vineyards round its flanks between the plain and the cliff of the cap. Every aspect is planted, so a cellar on the south face and one on the north make different wine from the same grape, and the slopes are dotted with small press-houses and cellars. Two smaller volcanic hills to the north-west, Ság and Kissomlyó, belong to the same district.
terroir.water: No river or lake shapes the wine. The Marcal is a small stream on the plain to the west, and Lake Balaton lies well to the south-east with no direct effect. The hill makes its own weather through height, exposure and wind rather than through water.

grapes.name: Juhfark
grapes.styles: The hill's own white, named for its long, tight bunch; neutral and hard when young, then smoky, honeyed and saline with age, always on a spine of high acid.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.styles: Dry, fiery and flinty here, with none of Tokaj's botrytis; the base of the hill's traditional-method sparkling wine as well as of serious still whites.

grapes.name: Hárslevelű
grapes.styles: Linden-blossom perfume and a rounder body that softens Juhfark and Furmint in the traditional hill blend; bottled alone it is the most fragrant wine on the hill.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.styles: Welschriesling under its Hungarian name: fresh, bitter-almond, easy whites for early drinking, and a component in the old field blends.

grapes.name: Tramini
grapes.styles: Traminer, grown in small amounts for an aromatic, slightly off-dry wine that stands apart from the hill's austere style.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A modern planting in a few cellars, made lean and mineral in the Somló manner rather than rich.

wines.note: Pale, lean, steely and smoky, with high acid and little fruit in youth, then honey, beeswax and a saline, flinty length after five to ten years. Serve cool rather than cold, with river fish, roast fowl or a hard cheese.
Dry and taut, green apple and flint, firmer and more mineral than most Tokaji dry Furmint, with a smoky finish from the basalt. A wine for oysters, pike-perch or roast pork.
The softest of the hill's whites, linden blossom and pear over the same volcanic smoke; drink within a few years with poultry, veal or mild cheese.
The traditional hill wine, a blend of Juhfark, Furmint, Hárslevelű and Olaszrizling, sometimes aged in old cask with a nutty edge; the style the Habsburg court would have known.
Traditional-method sparkling built on Furmint, aged years on its lees; bready, bone dry, high in acid and a credible stand-in for a grower Champagne by the glass.

made.viticulture: Small holdings are the hill's pattern, many of them a strip of rows above a press-house, divided among the villages round the base; Somlóvásárhely, Somlószőlős, Somlójenő and Doba are the names that recur. Vines are mostly on wires on steep, stony ground that was once terraced and walled by hand, and the slope keeps much of the work manual. Juhfark is demanding: its bunches are tight and its skins thin, so rot threatens in a wet autumn and the wind is the grower's ally. It is picked for acidity rather than sugar. Spring frost is less of a danger on the slopes than on the plain, because cold air drains off the hill. The ground itself keeps yields low, and the serious houses crop lower still for the wines meant to age.
made.winemaking: The old way belonged to the hill: grapes pressed in the press-house on the slope, fermented in the cellar beneath it and aged for a year or more in large old oak with a little air, which gave the wines their nutty, honeyed cast and their reputation for keeping. Modern cellars split the difference: stainless steel for the crisp bottlings, used barrels of several hundred litres for the serious Juhfark and Furmint, and malolactic conversion usually avoided so the acid stays bright. Lees contact is common, to give body to a grape that offers little fruit. Sweet wines are rare and botrytis is not sought. A traditional-method sparkling wine from Furmint, aged on its lees for years, has become one of the hill's calling cards in the twenty-first century.

law.classification: Somló is a wine district (borvidék) of the Balaton wine region (borrégió) and a protected designation of origin under European law, which Hungary writes as OEM, oltalom alatt álló eredetmegjelölés. The district's administrative name is Nagy-Somló; the name on labels is Somló or the adjective Somlói. The rules centre on white wine, with sparkling wine provided for, and the hill is a white district in all but name. Hungarian law carries no cru ranking of the Burgundian kind; a named site, a dűlő, may be printed under the rules the specification sets for it. The local hegyközség, the growers' community, administers the rules and the national wine authority holds the product specification.
tiers: OEM Somló (Somlói)
The protected designation of origin: grapes from the delimited slopes of Somló, Ság and Kissomlyó, in the varieties and at the yields the product specification sets
Balaton OEM and Balatonmelléki OFJ
The regional designation and the protected geographical indication the lake region's districts fall back on, with looser rules and more varieties
Dűlő
A named site on the label, printed under the rules the specification sets for it
labels: of Somló: the adjective the label carries
Great Somló, the district's administrative name
sheep's tail, the hill's own white grape
cellar; a pincészet is a winery

places.name: Somló hill
places.note: The volcanic butte itself, one vineyard hill planted on every face and crowned by a cliff of basalt and a ruined medieval castle. The south and south-west slopes are the warmest and give the fullest wines; the north and east faces are slower and keep more acid. Hundreds of small press-houses and cellars stand among the rows.

places.name: Somlóvásárhely
places.note: The old market town at the southern foot of the hill, the largest of the villages round it and the district's main road in.

places.name: Somlószőlős
places.note: The village whose name means Somló of the vines; its land climbs the hill's north-western side, and several of the serious estates keep cellars there.

places.name: Somlójenő
places.note: A small village at the foot of the hill whose rows run up the slope; one of the four communes whose land meets on Somló.

places.name: Doba
places.note: The village on the western side of the hill below the castle, with the ruined fortress above it; quieter and cooler sites.

places.name: Ság hill
places.note: A second, smaller basalt volcano near Celldömölk to the north-west, quarried in the last century so that much of its cone is cut away; the surviving slopes carry vineyards within the Nagy-Somló district.

places.name: Kissomlyó
places.note: Little Somló, a third low basalt hill between the other two, with a small vineyard area that shares the district's name and rules.

producers.name: Kreinbacher
producers.why: The estate that put traditional-method Furmint sparkling wine on Somló's map, alongside serious still Juhfark.

producers.name: Tornai
producers.why: One of the largest houses on the hill, with a full range from easy Olaszrizling to single-site Juhfark that shows the district at every price.

producers.name: Kolonics
producers.why: A small family cellar in the old manner, long cask ageing and wines that need years, the style the hill was known for.

producers.name: Somlói Apátsági Pince
producers.why: The abbey cellar tied to the Benedictines of Pannonhalma, a reminder that the church shaped Somló's vineyards for centuries.

exam: Know Somló as a single volcanic hill, the smallest district, white, with Juhfark the grape nobody else claims.
Place it: western Hungary, north-west of Lake Balaton, in the Balaton wine region, administratively Nagy-Somló.
Describe the style in a sentence: high acid, smoky, saline, slow to open, built to keep.
Hold the soils in order: basalt cap, tuff, Pannonian sand and clay, loess at the foot.
Carry the Habsburg wedding-night legend as a one-line story, never as a rule.
Know Furmint grows here dry and unbotrytised, and that it bases the hill's sparkling wine.
traps: Somló is not on Lake Balaton; Badacsony is. Both are basalt hills, which is the confusion.
Juhfark is a white grape; sheep's tail describes the bunch, not a colour.
Nagy-Somló and Somló name the same district: one is the administrative name, one the label.
Somlói Furmint is dry; do not reach for aszú, puttonyos or any Tokaj vocabulary here.
Kissomlyó, spelt with a y, is the little hill in the district; Somló is the big one.
The old course note calls the whites taut, smoky and ageworthy; that is right, and the acid is the reason.

cards.b: A single extinct volcano, a basalt-capped butte, standing alone in western Hungary north-west of Lake Balaton; the country's smallest wine district.

cards.f: Somló's signature grape, and what its name means
cards.b: Juhfark, sheep's tail, for its long tight bunch. A white grape: high acid, smoky, saline, slow to open.

cards.f: The four whites of the traditional Somló blend
cards.b: Juhfark, Furmint, Hárslevelű and Olaszrizling.

cards.f: Somló's soils, top to bottom
cards.b: Basalt cap, basalt tuff and ash, then Pannonian sand and clay; loess at the foot.

cards.f: The wine region (borrégió) that holds Somló
cards.b: Balaton. The district's administrative name is Nagy-Somló; labels say Somlói.

cards.f: The Somló legend worth one sentence
cards.b: The Habsburg court drank it and called it the wine of the wedding night, said to favour a male heir.

cards.f: Furmint on Somló: how does it differ from Tokaj?
cards.b: Dry, unbotrytised, flinty and smoky; also the base of the hill's traditional-method sparkling wine.

cards.f: Other hills inside the Nagy-Somló district
cards.b: Ság hill near Celldömölk and Kissomlyó, both small basalt volcanoes to the north-west.

questions.q: A white grape grown almost nowhere else takes its name from the shape of its bunch and gives the austere, smoky wine of this hill. Which grape?
questions.exp: Juhfark means sheep's tail, after its long tight bunch. Kéknyelű belongs to Badacsony, Ezerjó to Mór, and Leányka is an Eger and Transylvanian white.

questions.q: The hill's wines are labelled Somlói, but the district carries a longer administrative name. Give it.
questions.exp: Nagy means great, so the district is Great Somló and takes in the smaller hills of Ság and Kissomlyó as well as the main butte.

questions.q: What rock forms the cap of the hill and the stony soils of its slopes?
questions.exp: Somló is an eroded volcano with a basalt cap over tuff and ash; the growers credit it with the smoke and flint in the wines. Limestone is Villány's rock, granite breaks through at Mórágy near Szekszárd.

questions.q: Hungary groups its districts into six wine regions. Which one holds Somló?
questions.exp: Somló sits with Badacsony and the lake districts in the Balaton region, though the hill is well inland of the water. Pannon holds Villány and Szekszárd; Duna holds Kunság.

questions.q: Olaszrizling, the blending white of Somló's old field blends, is grown in Austria under which name?
questions.exp: Olasz means Italian, so the Hungarian name says Italian Riesling, and Austria's Welschriesling says foreign Riesling for the same grape. It is no relation of true Riesling: a neutral, fresh, bitter-almond white for early drinking.

questions.q: What does the word száraz mean on the label of a Somlói Furmint?
questions.exp: Száraz is dry; félszáraz is off-dry, félédes medium sweet and édes sweet. Somló makes its Furmint dry and without botrytis, so száraz is the word a guest sees most often on the hill's labels.

questions.q: Which grape forms the base of the traditional-method sparkling wine that modern Somló estates have made a speciality?
questions.exp: Furmint's high acid and modest fruit make a natural sparkling base, and on Somló it is grown dry with no botrytis. Juhfark is the still-wine signature; the bubbles lean on Furmint.

questions.q: A guest orders a young Somlói Juhfark. What is the wine most likely to show?
questions.exp: Juhfark is neutral and hard in youth, all acid and volcanic smoke, and only with years does honey and beeswax arrive. Lychee is Gewürztraminer's mark, blackcurrant Cabernet's, petrol aged Riesling's.

regions.name: Szekszárd
regions.summary: Szekszárd is the red-wine town of southern Transdanubia, on loess hills that rise from the west bank of the Danube's flood plain in Tolna county. Kékfrankos leads, Kadarka is the old native red the district has revived, and Merlot and the two Cabernets fill out the blends. Its Bikavér is the only one outside Eger allowed the name, and its rules are stricter on the native grapes. The wines are warmer, rounder and spicier than Eger's, with a southern softness, and rosé and the pale red called fuxli are local habits. It belongs to the Pannon wine region with Villány, Pécs and Tolna.

terroir.climate: Warm and sunny, among the warmest districts in Hungary after Villány, with the continental swing between winter cold and summer heat softened by air that comes up the Danube corridor from the south. Rain is moderate and falls mostly in early summer; autumns are long and usually dry, which lets Cabernet ripen and keeps Kadarka's thin skins sound. Hail is the recurring hazard of the hills.
terroir.soils: Deep loess, wind-blown silt laid down in the ice ages, tens of metres thick in places and carved into sunken lanes and gullies. Beneath it lies red clay, and in the south around Mórágy an old granite breaks the surface. Loess drains well, warms quickly and holds enough water through dry spells; it gives red wines that are soft in tannin and full in body rather than hard.
terroir.topography: The Szekszárd hills are the eastern edge of the Transdanubian hill country, a ridge of loess rising to around three hundred metres and cut into valleys that run down to the town and the plain. The best sites are the south- and east-facing valley sides above the town, and the famous names are valley names: Iván-völgy, Baranya-völgy, Porkoláb-völgy, Görögszó, Bati-kereszt. East of the town the land drops to the Sárköz, the old flood plain.
terroir.water: The Danube runs a few kilometres to the east beyond the Sárköz, and the Sió, which drains Lake Balaton, joins it close by. Neither touches the vineyards, but the river valley is the channel through which warm southern air reaches the hills, and the plain beside it lifts the morning humidity that makes hail and rot the district's worries.

grapes.name: Kékfrankos
grapes.styles: Blaufränkisch under its Hungarian name: the frame of Szekszárdi Bikavér and the district's most planted red, sour cherry and pepper on bright acid, rounder here than in Eger or Sopron.

grapes.name: Kadarka
grapes.styles: The old native red, pale, light and peppery with raspberry and paprika spice; nearly lost, now replanted from selected clones and compulsory in the town's Bikavér.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Ripens easily on the loess and gives the plush middle of the Bordeaux-style blends and of many Bikavérs.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Fragrant, ripe and fine-tannined on these hills; bottled alone by the serious houses and a frequent fourth grape in Bikavér.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The last picked; full and cedary in warm years, blended more often than bottled alone.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: A soft, juicy filler for everyday reds and rosé.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.styles: The district's everyday white, fresh and bitter-almond, a sideline in a red town.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A little, mostly for simple steel-fermented whites and sparkling base.

wines.note: A blend of at least four varieties built on Kékfrankos with Kadarka compulsory and a year in wood; spicy, medium to full, sour cherry and pepper with a rounder frame than Eger's. Serve at cellar temperature with paprika-rich dishes, lamb or roast duck.
Pale, light and fragrant: raspberry, white pepper and a lick of paprika, low tannin and lively acid. Serve a touch cool with charcuterie, goulash or grilled sausage.
Medium-bodied, sour cherry, black pepper and a soft loess roundness, oak-aged in the serious bottlings; the district's most reliable red for pork, game birds and stews.
Merlot and the Cabernets, often with Kékfrankos, aged in barrique: ripe, warm and plush, the district's answer to Villány and a match for beef and roast lamb.
Dry, pale and strawberry-fresh, usually from Kékfrankos, Merlot or Zweigelt; the district's calling card by the glass and a summer wine for salads and fish.
The local siller, a short-macerated light red between rosé and red, fox-coloured as the name says; drunk young and cool with the everyday table.

made.viticulture: The vineyards ride the valley sides above the town and the villages south and west of it, Sióagárd, Szálka, Bátaszék and Mórágy, with rows on wires on loess that holds its shape in steep cuts. Kékfrankos is the workhorse: late to bud, late to ripen, generous if allowed, so bunch-thinning and green harvest are routine for the serious wines. Kadarka is the trouble: it ripens late, its thin-skinned berries rot in a damp September and it gives little colour, so it was nearly abandoned under the socialist plantings and has been brought back through clone selection and growers willing to pick in several passes. Merlot and the Cabernets ripen reliably here, Cabernet Franc especially. Hail nets are more common than they were. Harvest runs from late August for the rosé base into October for Cabernet Sauvignon. Old-vine Kadarka on the loess is the district's treasure.
made.winemaking: Red winemaking of the warm-country kind: destemmed fruit, pumping over or punching down in steel or open vats, two to three weeks on the skins for the Bordeaux varieties, shorter and gentler for Kadarka, whose colour and tannin come easily out of balance. Bikavér is assembled with Kékfrankos the frame, Kadarka the spice and the Bordeaux varieties filling in, and the rules ask at least a year in wood. Oak is the modern mark: barrique for the Cabernets and Merlot, larger and older casks for Kadarka and Kékfrankos, and the better houses have pulled back from new wood. Rosé is made by direct pressing or a few hours' maceration and bottled early; fuxli, the local siller, is a short-macerated light red drunk young and cool. Whites are a sideline, fermented in steel and sold young.

law.classification: Szekszárd is a wine district (borvidék) of the Pannon wine region and a protected designation of origin, OEM in Hungarian, with its product specification lodged with the national wine authority and administered through the local hegyközség. Its special rule is Bikavér: Szekszárdi Bikavér is a blend of at least four varieties with Kékfrankos the largest share at a minimum of 45 per cent and Kadarka compulsory at a minimum of 5 per cent, the rest drawn from the permitted list, and the wine spends at least a year in wood. A Prémium Bikavér carries a lower yield cap than the base blend. Beyond that, a named dűlő may be printed under the rules the specification sets. The specification's fourth version applies to wines marketed from 15 March 2024.

Szekszárdi Bikavér
At least four varieties; Kékfrankos at least 45 per cent, Kadarka at least 5 per cent; the rest from the permitted list; at least a year in wood
Szekszárdi Prémium Bikavér

labels: of Szekszárd: the adjective on the label
bull's blood: the district's protected blend, shared only with Eger
the local siller, a light red between rosé and red
a short-macerated pale red, darker than rosé

places.name: Szekszárd town and its valleys
places.note: The town sits where the loess hills meet the plain, and its vineyards climb the valleys behind it, each a named site with its own exposure. The Benedictine abbey founded here in 1061 by King Béla I kept vines for centuries, and the composer Liszt, who visited in 1846, praised the red wine. The valley names are the district's crus in all but law.

places.name: Iván-völgy
places.note: The best-known valley above the town, loess slopes that give full Kékfrankos and Bordeaux-variety wines.

places.name: Görögszó
places.note: A warm site on the hills above the town, a name that appears on serious Kékfrankos and Kadarka labels.

places.name: Bati-kereszt
places.note: A valley-side vineyard above the town named for a wayside cross, a name that recurs on the leading houses' red labels.

places.name: Baranya-völgy
places.note: A valley among the hills, deep loess and old vines, a source of single-site Kadarka.

places.name: Porkoláb-völgy
places.note: A valley among the hills behind the town whose name recurs on single-vineyard bottlings from the leading houses.

places.name: Sióagárd
places.note: A village at the north-western edge of the hills where the Sió comes down to the Danube, with its own vineyards and a historic row of press-houses and cellars.

places.name: Szálka
places.note: A hill village south-west of the town settled by German speakers in the eighteenth century, whose cellars and slopes feed the district's reds.

places.name: Bátaszék
places.note: A town at the southern end of the district where the hills meet the plain, with vineyards on the last loess slopes before the Danube's old marshes.

places.name: Mórágy
places.note: The district's southern oddity, where an ancient granite block breaks through the loess and gives a few vineyards a harder, stonier footing.

places.name: Sárköz
places.note: Not a vineyard but the flood plain east of the town between the hills and the Danube, once marsh, now farmland and famous for its embroidery; it is the open ground through which the river's humid air reaches the slopes.

producers.name: Heimann
producers.why: The family estate that made the case for Kadarka and Kékfrankos as the district's true voice, with old vines and restraint in the cellar.

producers.name: Takler
producers.why: A large modern estate whose ripe Bordeaux-variety reds and Bikavér carried Szekszárd's name abroad in the 2000s.

producers.name: Vesztergombi
producers.why: A traditional house known for Bikavér and Kadarka, with cellars in the old lanes of the town.

producers.name: Vida
producers.why: A small estate whose single-vineyard Bikavér and Kékfrankos show the valley sites at their most serious.

producers.name: Eszterbauer
producers.why: A Kadarka specialist working old plantings, the bottle to pour when a guest asks what the native grape tastes like.

producers.name: Bodri
producers.why: A large estate with a visitor centre above the town and a wide range, the easy introduction to the district's styles.

exam: Know Szekszárd as the second Bikavér district, and the stricter one: Kékfrankos the frame, Kadarka compulsory, four varieties, a year in wood.
Place it: southern Transdanubia, Tolna county, loess hills west of the Danube, Pannon wine region.
Hold the soil in one word, loess, and what it does: soft tannin, full body, warmth.
Be able to describe Kadarka: pale, light, peppery, thin-skinned and hard to grow.
Know the local pale red, fuxli or siller, and that rosé is the district's glass-pour calling card.
Compare with Eger: warmer, rounder, more southern; Eger is cooler, more acid, volcanic.
traps: Szekszárd is loess, not volcanic; Eger's Bikavér grows on tuff. Same name, different ground.
Kadarka is compulsory in Szekszárdi Bikavér and only permitted in Egri Bikavér; the Kékfrankos minimum is also higher here.
Fuxli is a siller, a light red, not a rosé in the strict sense, though it is listed with the pinks.
Szekszárd lies west of the Danube; Kunság's sand lies east of it. Do not put the loess hills on the plain.
Villány is south and warmer still; Szekszárd is the northern, Kékfrankos-led half of the Pannon pair.
The old course note names Kékfrankos, Kadarka, Merlot and the Cabernets; that is right, and Bikavér is the blend that binds them.

cards.f: Szekszárdi Bikavér: the blend rule in one breath
cards.b: At least four varieties; Kékfrankos at least 45 per cent; Kadarka at least 5 per cent and compulsory; the rest from the permitted list; at least a year in wood.

cards.f: Szekszárd's soil and what it gives
cards.b: Deep wind-blown loess over red clay: warm, well drained, soft tannins and full body. Granite breaks through only at Mórágy.

cards.f: The two Hungarian districts allowed to label Bikavér
cards.b: Eger and Szekszárd. Eger's is volcanic and cooler; Szekszárd's is loess and warmer, with Kadarka compulsory.

cards.f: Describe Kadarka in a sentence
cards.b: The old native red: pale, light-bodied, peppery and raspberry-scented, thin-skinned and rot-prone, so hard to grow and nearly lost.

cards.f: What is fuxli?
cards.b: Szekszárd's siller: a short-macerated light red between rosé and red, named for its fox colour, drunk young and cool.

cards.f: Szekszárd: county, river, wine region
cards.b: Tolna county, on loess hills west of the Danube and the Sárköz plain; Pannon wine region with Villány, Pécs and Tolna.

cards.f: Szekszárd's famous valley vineyards
cards.b: Iván-völgy, Görögszó, Bati-kereszt, Baranya-völgy and Porkoláb-völgy: named sites above the town, the district's crus in all but law.

cards.f: Szekszárd against Eger in two lines
cards.b: Szekszárd: loess, warmer, rounder, Kadarka required. Eger: volcanic tuff, cooler, higher acid, Kékfrankos minimum lower, Kadarka optional.

questions.q: One grape is compulsory in Szekszárdi Bikavér but only permitted in Egri Bikavér. Name it.
questions.exp: Szekszárd wrote its native red into the rule at a minimum of five per cent, where Eger lists it among the options. Kékfrankos is the frame in both.

questions.q: How many grape varieties, at the least, must go into a Szekszárdi Bikavér?
questions.exp: Four is the floor, with Kékfrankos the largest share and Kadarka compulsory. Eger fixes its own numbers for Egri Bikavér, so learn the two rules apart rather than as one.

questions.q: What soil covers the Szekszárd hills and gives the reds their soft, full frame?
questions.exp: Wind-blown loess lies tens of metres deep over red clay. Basalt is Somló's and Badacsony's rock, limestone underlies Villány, and granite shows only at Mórágy in the district's south.

questions.q: Hungary groups its wine districts into six regions. Which one holds Szekszárd?
questions.exp: Pannon takes in Szekszárd, Villány, Pécs and Tolna in the south of Transdanubia. Duna is the sandy plain; Felső-Magyarország is Eger, Mátra and Bükk.

questions.q: Szekszárd's cellars pour a pale, short-macerated red that sits between rosé and red. What is it called locally?
questions.exp: Fuxli, named for its fox colour, is the Szekszárd word for a siller, the Central European light red made with a few hours on the skins and drunk young and cool.

questions.q: The Sárköz plain east of the town is the old flood plain of which river?
questions.exp: Szekszárd stands where the loess hills meet the Danube's plain; the Sió, draining Balaton, joins the river just to the north. The Tisza bounds Kunság on the far side of the plain, the Drava is the southern border, and the Hernád comes down from Slovakia to the Tisza in the north-east.

questions.q: Which grape must make up the largest share of a Szekszárdi Bikavér, with a minimum of 45 per cent?
questions.exp: Kékfrankos is Blaufränkisch under its Hungarian name and the frame of both Bikavérs; Szekszárd sets the higher floor. Kadarka supplies the spice at a minimum of five per cent.

questions.q: A guest asks what a varietal Szekszárdi Kadarka will be like. Which description fits?
opts: Pale colour, light tannin, peppery spice
Deep colour, firm tannin and blackcurrant
questions.exp: Kadarka is thin-skinned and gives little colour or tannin, with raspberry and white pepper on lively acid. Deep blackcurrant describes Cabernet; chocolate and vanilla a heavily oaked Merlot.

regions.name: Villány
regions.summary: Villány is Hungary's warmest wine district, in the far south on a limestone ridge that runs east to west a few kilometres from the Croatian border. It is red country: Cabernet Franc is its flagship and the district's own designation, Villányi Franc, belongs to it; Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Kékfrankos and Portugieser, the light red once called Kékoportó, make up the rest. In 2006 the district adopted Hungary's first district quality tiers, Classicus and Prémium, with yield and ageing fixed for each; Super Prémium joined later. The wines are ripe, full, oak-aged and the most Bordeaux-like in the country. Cellar rows at Villánykövesd and Palkonya and the Villány-Siklós wine road are its visiting face.

terroir.climate: Sub-Mediterranean inside a continental frame: among the most sunshine and the warmest growing season of any Hungarian district, with air arriving from the Adriatic side across the Drava plain. Winters are still cold, but spring comes early, summer is hot and dry, and autumn long and settled, so Cabernet Sauvignon ripens fully in most years, which it cannot be trusted to do further north. Heat and drought stress on the thin hill soils are the modern concern.
terroir.soils: Limestone and dolomite of the Villány hills, Triassic and Jurassic rock, with a mantle of loess over most of the slopes and pockets of red clay weathered from the stone. The loess gives body and softness, the limestone beneath drains and lends freshness and a finer tannin; the best sites are where the mantle is thin and the roots find the rock.
terroir.topography: A low ridge rising abruptly from the plain and running east to west for some twenty-five kilometres, with Szársomlyó above Nagyharsány its highest point at over four hundred metres. Vines occupy the south-facing foot and lower slopes from Siklós in the west through Nagyharsány, Palkonya and Villánykövesd to Villány at the eastern end. The south face takes sun all day; the north side is forest.
terroir.water: The Drava, the border with Croatia, crosses the plain a short way south, and the Danube lies to the east; neither reaches the vineyards. Their plains matter as the open channel through which warm southern air arrives, and the district is otherwise dry, with the water the vines need held in the loess.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: The flagship: ripe blackcurrant and black cherry, graphite, violets and fine tannin, fuller than the Loire's and without its green edge; bottled alone as Villányi Franc under the strictest rules.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripens fully here as almost nowhere else in Hungary; cedar, cassis and firm structure, alone or leading the Bordeaux-style blends.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The earliest of the Bordeaux three, plush and chocolatey, the softener in the cuvées and a varietal in cooler sites.

grapes.name: Kékfrankos
grapes.styles: Blaufränkisch under its Hungarian name: fresher, peppery reds and rosé, and the native note in many blends.

grapes.name: Portugieser
grapes.styles: The light, juicy, low-tannin red the district drank before Cabernet arrived, labelled Kékoportó until European naming rules retired the word; served young and cool.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: Easy, fruity reds and rosé for the everyday Classicus tier.

grapes.name: Kadarka
grapes.styles: A little of the old native red survives, pale and spicy, more curiosity than core here.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.styles: The white of the Siklós end of the ridge, fresh and bitter-almond, with Hárslevelű beside it.

wines.note: Cabernet Franc alone, made to the Prémium or Super Prémium rules: ripe cassis and black cherry, graphite, violets, full body and polished oak, built to age a decade. Decant, serve at cellar temperature with lamb, beef or aged hard cheese.
Cedar, blackcurrant and firm tannin, the most Bordeaux-like red in Hungary; the Prémium bottlings need years and want roast beef or game.
The Bordeaux-style blend of the two Cabernets and Merlot, often with Kékfrankos, aged in barrique; warm, plush and long, the district's grand bottle for a table of red-meat eaters.
Light, soft, juicy and low in tannin, the traditional young red of the Swabian cellars, once sold as Kékoportó; serve cool with charcuterie, poultry or the cellar's own pogácsa.
Medium-bodied, sour cherry and pepper, riper than Sopron's and brighter than the Cabernets; a wine for paprika dishes and pork.
Dry, pale pink, strawberry and cream, usually from Kékfrankos, Portugieser or Merlot; the Classicus tier's summer glass.
Olaszrizling and Hárslevelű from the western end of the ridge around Siklós, fresh and simple, the district's reminder that it once grew more white than red.

made.viticulture: Vines on wires with a vertical canopy on the south-facing lower slopes; leaf-plucking and row orientation are now about shade rather than exposure, because sun is not the limiting factor. The district's rules tie quality to yield: Classicus allows the generous crop of an everyday wine, Prémium is capped at sixty hectolitres per hectare and Super Prémium at thirty-five, so cluster thinning and green harvest are part of the calendar for the top wines. Cabernet Franc buds and ripens a little ahead of Cabernet Sauvignon and suits the site because its tannin ripens before the sugar runs away; Merlot is earliest and can turn flabby in a hot year. Portugieser and Kékfrankos are picked first, in early September, the Cabernets in late September or October, largely by hand on the slopes. Drought and heat are the growing worries, and the limestone's sharp drainage cuts both ways. The rootstock pioneer Zsigmond Teleki, who died in 1910, bred his phylloxera-resistant stocks in a Villány nursery, and the district's replanting rode on them.
made.winemaking: Bordeaux methods adapted to a warmer place: destemming, a cold soak in many cellars, fermentation in steel or wooden vats with pumping over, two to four weeks on the skins for the Cabernets, then malolactic conversion in barrel. Barriques of French and Hungarian oak are the signature; the reputation of the 1990s was built on ripe fruit and new wood, and the leading houses now use a share of used barrels and larger casks for balance. The tiers fix the time: Prémium wines spend at least a year in wood as the general rule, Super Prémium at least two years with a year of it in wood before release. Villányi Franc is Cabernet Franc alone, made only to the Prémium or Super Prémium rules, never blended. Portugieser is made as a quick, fruity red with little or no oak, rosé by direct pressing. The cellars are the old Swabian ones cut into the loess at Villánykövesd and Palkonya, cool enough to age wine without machinery.

law.classification: Villány is a wine district of the Pannon wine region and a protected designation of origin, OEM in Hungarian. In 2006 its growers' community adopted the first formal quality tiers inside a Hungarian district, marked DHC, Districtus Hungaricus Controllatus: Classicus, the everyday wines, and Prémium, with yield capped at sixty hectolitres per hectare and at least a year in wood as the general rule. Super Prémium, capped at thirty-five hectolitres per hectare with at least two years' ageing and a year of it in wood, was added when the rules were revised in the following decade. Villányi Franc, the district's own designation for a wine of Cabernet Franc alone made to the Prémium or Super Prémium rules, was first granted for the 2015 harvest. A named vineyard may be printed under the rules the specification sets, and the hegyközség polices the whole.

places.name: Villány
places.note: The town that names the district, on the eastern half of the ridge, with its cellar street and most of the leading estates. Its named sites on the south-facing slope are the district's best-known vineyards and appear on Super Prémium labels.

places.name: Jammertal
places.note: A warm south-facing site above the town whose German name, valley of lament, recalls the Swabian settlers; a source of top Cabernet Franc.

places.name: Kopár
places.note: The bare slope, a stony limestone site above Villány that gives some of the most concentrated Cabernet wines in Hungary.

places.name: Ördögárok
places.note: The devil's ditch, a steep site on the hillside above the town, planted mostly to the Bordeaux varieties.

places.name: Villánykövesd
places.note: The village just west of Villány on the Siklós road, whose terraced rows of eighteenth-century Swabian press-houses and cellars, cut into the loess, are the district's most photographed sight and still hold ageing wine.

places.name: Palkonya
places.note: A small village in the hills north-west of Villánykövesd with a protected row of whitewashed cellars, where several young estates have settled.

places.name: Nagyharsány
places.note: The village under Szársomlyó's south face, the warmest ground on the ridge, with an old quarry turned sculpture park above it and serious Cabernet below.

places.name: Kisharsány
places.note: The neighbouring village at the western foot of Szársomlyó, home to one of the district's larger modern estates and its hillside vineyards.

places.name: Siklós
places.note: The castle town at the western end of the ridge, the other name in the Villány-Siklós wine road opened in 1994, the first in Hungary; the Siklós end traditionally grew more white, Olaszrizling and Hárslevelű, than red.

places.name: Szársomlyó
places.note: The highest hill of the ridge, bare limestone on its south face and a nature reserve for a rare wildflower, with the warmest vineyards of the district on the slopes below it.

producers.name: Gere
producers.why: The house whose Kopár cuvée and varietal Cabernet Franc gave Villány its modern reputation and the model for Villányi Franc.

producers.name: Bock
producers.why: One of the district's founding modern estates, with cellars under the town and Bordeaux-style cuvées that set the Prémium standard.

producers.name: Vylyan
producers.why: A large estate at Kisharsány under Szársomlyó, known for varietal reds and a willingness to experiment.

producers.name: Sauska
producers.why: A modern estate in Villány with polished Cabernet Franc and blends, and a sister cellar in Tokaj.

producers.name: Tiffán
producers.why: An old Villány family house that kept the Swabian cellar tradition alive through the socialist years.

producers.name: Csányi
producers.why: A large estate holding the historic Teleki cellars, named for the rootstock breeder who worked in Villány until his death in 1910.

producers.name: Malatinszky
producers.why: A smaller estate known for single-vineyard Cabernet Franc and for championing organic work on the ridge.

exam: Know Villány as Hungary's warmest district and its Cabernet Franc capital, in the far south on limestone under loess.
Hold the three tiers and their numbers: Classicus, Prémium (sixty hectolitres, a year in wood), Super Prémium (thirty-five, two years with a year in wood).
Know Villányi Franc: Cabernet Franc alone, Prémium or Super Prémium only, first granted for the 2015 harvest.
Place it: Pannon wine region, Baranya county, the ridge from Siklós to Villány, the Drava and Croatia just south.
Know Portugieser as the old light red once labelled Kékoportó, and why the name changed.
Be able to say why Cabernet Sauvignon ripens here and not in Eger: sunshine hours and a long settled autumn.
traps: Villányi Franc is Cabernet Franc alone, not a blend and not Cabernet Sauvignon; the name hides the grape.
Kékoportó and Portugieser are one grape; the old name is off the label, not off the vine.
Villány's rock is limestone, not the volcanic ground of Somló, Badacsony, Eger or Tokaj.
Szársomlyó, the ridge's high hill, is not Somló; a shared syllable is the whole connection.
The tiers are the district's own; Hungarian law has no national cru ranking, and other districts use different words.
The old course note calls Villány Hungary's warmest reds; that is right, and sub-Mediterranean is the word to use.
say: VEE-lahny, the ny as in canyon

cards.f: Villány in one sentence
cards.b: Hungary's warmest district, far south on a limestone ridge near Croatia, famous for Cabernet Franc and Bordeaux-style reds; Pannon wine region.

cards.f: Villány's three tiers and their numbers
cards.b: Classicus: everyday, highest yields. Prémium: sixty hectolitres per hectare, a year in wood. Super Prémium: thirty-five, at least two years with a year in wood.

cards.f: What is Villányi Franc?
cards.b: The district's own designation, first granted for the 2015 harvest: Cabernet Franc alone, made to the Prémium or Super Prémium rules, never blended.

cards.f: Villány's soils, top to bottom
cards.b: Triassic and Jurassic limestone and dolomite under a mantle of loess with pockets of red clay; warmth from the loess, freshness from the rock.

cards.f: Kékoportó: what is it now?
cards.b: Portugieser. The old Hungarian name was retired from labels under European naming rules; the grape makes Villány's light, juicy traditional red.

cards.f: The year Villány adopted its tiers
cards.b: 2006, the first formal quality classification inside a Hungarian district, under the DHC mark; Super Prémium joined with a later revision.

cards.f: Hungary's first wine road
cards.b: The Villány-Siklós wine road, opened in 1994, along the south face of the ridge from the castle town to the cellar villages.

cards.f: The ridge's highest point and its village
cards.b: Szársomlyó, over four hundred metres, above Nagyharsány; its south face holds the district's warmest vineyards.

cards.f: Villány's cellar villages
cards.b: Villánykövesd and Palkonya: rows of Swabian press-houses cut into loess, eighteenth century, still used for ageing.

questions.q: A bottle is labelled Villányi Franc. What share of the wine must be Cabernet Franc?
questions.exp: Villányi Franc is a varietal rule, Cabernet Franc alone with no blending, and only at Prémium or Super Prémium level. The lower figures belong to other countries' varietal thresholds.

questions.q: Villány's limestone ridge runs a few kilometres from Hungary's border with which country?
questions.exp: The ridge lies in Baranya county in Hungary's far south, a few kilometres from the Croatian border, with the Drava on the plain beyond. Warm air arriving from that side is why Villány ripens Cabernet Sauvignon as no other Hungarian district can.

questions.q: What is the maximum yield for a Villány wine at Super Prémium level?
questions.exp: Super Prémium is capped at thirty-five hectolitres per hectare with at least two years' ageing and a year of it in wood; Prémium allows sixty. The highest figure is far above either capped tier.

questions.q: Villány's traditional light red is now labelled Portugieser. Under which older Hungarian name was it sold?
questions.exp: Kék means blue, and Kékoportó was the Hungarian name for Portugieser until European naming rules retired it. Kékfrankos is Blaufränkisch, Kéknyelű a white of Badacsony, Kadarka the pale native red.

questions.q: In which year did Villány adopt its tiered quality system under the DHC mark, the first such system inside a Hungarian district?
questions.exp: The growers' community fixed yields and ageing for Classicus and Prémium from 2006; Super Prémium joined with a later revision and Villányi Franc followed for the 2015 harvest.

questions.q: Which hill above Nagyharsány is the highest point of the Villány ridge?
questions.exp: Szársomlyó rises over four hundred metres with bare limestone on its south face and the district's warmest vineyards below. Badacsony, Szent György-hegy and Csobánc are basalt hills of the Balaton region.

questions.q: Hungary's first wine road, opened in 1994, runs along the ridge from Villány to which castle town?
questions.exp: Siklós anchors the western end of the ridge, where the vineyards once grew more white than red; the Villány-Siklós wine road links its castle to the cellar villages in the east.

questions.q: What bedrock lies beneath the loess on the Villány hills?
questions.exp: The ridge is Triassic and Jurassic limestone and dolomite; the loess mantle gives body and the rock below gives freshness. Basalt is the Balaton hills' rock, granite shows at Mórágy, and red sandstone is the Permian ground of the Balaton uplands around Csopak.

regions.name: Kunság
regions.summary: Kunság is the great sandy plain between the Danube and the Tisza, Hungary's largest wine district by far and the engine of its everyday wine. Vines went there after phylloxera, because the louse cannot live in quartz sand, and ungrafted vines still stand. The climate is extreme: among the hottest summers and coldest winters in the country, with abundant sunshine, little rain and frost as the constant hazard. The wines are light, fresh and simple: aromatic whites from Cserszegi Fűszeres, Irsai Olivér and Olaszrizling, sparkling base from Arany Sárfehér around Izsák, and soft reds from Kékfrankos, Kadarka and Zweigelt. Kiskőrös, Kecskemét, Izsák and Soltvadkert are its towns, and it sits in the Duna wine region.

terroir.climate: The most continental in the country: summers of fierce heat and drought, winters that can kill vines in the open, more sunshine than almost anywhere else in Hungary and among the lowest rainfall, well under six hundred millimetres in a normal year. Spring and autumn frosts strike the flat land because cold air has nowhere to drain. The sand heats fast by day and cools fast by night, which keeps some freshness in the whites.
terroir.soils: Wind-blown quartz sand, old dunes fixed by planting, over the alluvium of the Danube and the Tisza, with lime-rich patches, pockets of loess and, in the hollows, alkaline soda flats where little grows. The high quartz content is the reason phylloxera cannot tunnel here, so vines may be planted on their own roots. Sand is poor, drains instantly and reflects heat; it gives light wines and demands water.
terroir.topography: Flat: the Alföld, the Great Plain, barely a hundred metres above sea level, with low sand ridges and shallow depressions the only relief. Vineyards are scattered in large blocks among orchards and arable land rather than gathered on slopes, which is why the atlas gives the district one locator and no boundary. The Danube bounds it to the west and the Tisza to the east.
terroir.water: The Danube on the west and the Tisza on the east define the district and the Duna wine region, but the vines sit on the dry sand ridge between them, above both rivers' flood plains. Irrigation is used where the rules allow it, and the water table under the sand has been falling, which is the long-term worry.

grapes.name: Cserszegi Fűszeres
grapes.styles: A spicy, Muscat-scented crossing of Irsai Olivér and Traminer bred at Cserszegtomaj in 1960 for the plain: fresh, aromatic, early-drinking whites, the district's signature glass.

grapes.name: Irsai Olivér
grapes.styles: An early-ripening aromatic crossing, grapey and floral, bottled young and often with a touch of sugar; one parent of Cserszegi Fűszeres.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.styles: Welschriesling under its Hungarian name, the plain's workhorse dry white, light and bitter-almond.

grapes.name: Arany Sárfehér
grapes.styles: An old white of the plain, neutral and high in acid, the historic base of Hungarian sparkling wine, with its own protected name around Izsák.

grapes.name: Ezerjó
grapes.styles: An old Hungarian white, crisp and neutral here, grown for everyday wine; its serious home is Mór.

grapes.name: Kövidinka
grapes.styles: A frost-hardy old variety of the sand, giving simple soft whites and surviving in old plantings.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Planted for commercial dry whites and sparkling base, clean and steel-fermented.

grapes.name: Kékfrankos
grapes.styles: The plain's main red, light and juicy on sand, fruity young reds and rosé; a few estates make a fuller version from old vines.

grapes.name: Kadarka
grapes.styles: The native red survives in old sand vineyards, pale, spicy and light, and a handful of growers bottle it alone.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: Soft, dark-fruited filler for everyday reds and rosé.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripens on the hot sand into simple, soft reds without the structure it finds in Villány.

wines.note: Pale, intensely aromatic, Muscat and spice with a soft, off-dry or dry finish; serve cold, young, with spring rolls, light salads or on its own on a terrace.
Grapey, floral and light, often slightly sweet, the plain's summer white; cold, young, with fruit or nothing at all.
Light, dry, bitter-almond and fresh, the carafe white of Hungarian tables; chilled with river fish and paprika chicken.
Tank-method sparkling from the neutral, acid white of Izsák, clean and simple, the base of much Hungarian fizz; a glass for an aperitif.
Light, fruity and soft, sour cherry without the pepper and grip of the hill versions; serve lightly cool with everyday dishes.
Pale, spicy and light from old sand vineyards, the plain's claim to the native grape; cool, with goulash or charcuterie.
Pale, strawberry-fresh and simple from Kékfrankos or Zweigelt, bottled early and drunk young.

made.viticulture: Vines on sand are planted on their own roots, which is the district's oddity, and they stand mostly on wires in wide rows for machine work; the old low bush vines and the sand-dune plantings of the first replanting have largely gone. Frost protection is the first concern: sites on the low ridges rather than the hollows and late pruning. Drought is the second: drip irrigation is used where the rules allow it. Yields are high by hill standards, and the crop is largely machine-harvested, early in the day in the heat, to keep the aromatic whites fresh. Crossings bred for the plain are the district's grapes: Cserszegi Fűszeres, Irsai Olivér, Zenit, Generosa and Bianca were raised for hardiness, early ripening and aroma. Kadarka survives in old plantings. Birds and spring frost take their share.
made.winemaking: Volume winemaking done cleanly: quick pressing, cold settling, cool fermentation in stainless steel with selected yeasts to hold the Muscat-like aromatics of Cserszegi and Irsai, and early bottling with a little residual sugar in the commercial styles. Arany Sárfehér, neutral and high in acid, is the historic base wine for Hungarian sparkling, and Izsák holds its own protected name for it, most of it made by the tank method. Reds are soft, destemmed, briefly macerated and rarely oaked for long; Kékfrankos and Zweigelt give fruity, early-drinking wines and rosé. The large cooperatives and bottlers of Kecskemét, Kiskőrös and Soltvadkert handle most of the fruit; a handful of estates make the case for the sand with old-vine Kadarka and serious Kékfrankos.

law.classification: Kunság is a wine district of the Duna wine region, beside Hajós-Baja and Csongrád, and a protected designation of origin, OEM Kunság or Kunsági, with the product specification held by the national authority and run through the local hegyközségek. Much of the plain's wine goes out instead under the geographical indication Duna-Tisza közi OFJ, the PGI for the land between the rivers, which allows more varieties and higher yields, and a regional PDO named Duna covers the three districts together. Izsáki Arany Sárfehér is a separate protected name of its own around Izsák, tied to sparkling wine. The district is divided into sub-districts, körzet, named for their towns: Kiskőrös, Kecskemét-Kiskunfélegyháza, Izsák, Cegléd, Monor, Jászság, Kiskunhalas-Kiskunmajsa and the strips along each river.

OEM Duna

OFJ Duna-Tisza közi

from between the Danube and the Tisza: the PGI of the plain

places.name: Kiskőrös
places.note: The vine town of the plain, with one of the largest vineyard areas of any Hungarian settlement and a cooperative tradition; the poet Sándor Petőfi was born here in 1823. Its sub-district is the heart of the sand.

places.name: Kecskemét
places.note: The city of the plain and the seat of the Kecskemét-Kiskunfélegyháza sub-district, famous for apricots and the apricot brandy pálinka as much as for wine; its large wineries bottle much of the district's volume.

places.name: Izsák
places.note: A town on the western side of the district whose neutral, high-acid Arany Sárfehér is the historic base of Hungarian sparkling wine and carries its own protected name.

places.name: Soltvadkert
places.note: A wine town south of Kiskőrös with a lake beside it, home to some of the plain's largest family bottlers and a fair share of its aromatic whites.

places.name: Kiskunhalas
places.note: A town in the dry south of the district, with Kiskunmajsa its sub-district partner, where frost-hardy old varieties and own-rooted vines persist.

places.name: Cegléd and Monor
places.note: The northern sub-districts towards Budapest; Monor keeps a cellar village of hundreds of press-houses on a low hill, a reminder that the plain's wine was once made by the family and not the cooperative.

places.name: Jászság
places.note: The north-eastern corner of the district towards the Tisza, the land of the Jász people settled in the Middle Ages, with scattered vineyards on sandy ridges.

producers.name: Frittmann
producers.why: A Soltvadkert family house that showed the sand can give clean, serious varietal whites and reds, with Cserszegi Fűszeres its calling card.

producers.name: Font
producers.why: A Soltvadkert estate with a wide range of aromatic whites and soft reds, a reliable picture of what the plain does well.

producers.name: Szentpéteri
producers.why: A Kiskőrös house with old-vine Kadarka and Kékfrankos that argues for the plain's reds.

exam: Know Kunság as the sandy plain between the Danube and the Tisza, the largest district, in the Duna wine region.
Hold the phylloxera story: quartz sand, no louse, own-rooted vines, the replanting after the 1880s.
Name the plain's grapes: Cserszegi Fűszeres, Irsai Olivér, Olaszrizling, Arany Sárfehér; Kékfrankos, Kadarka, Zweigelt.
Know Izsák and Arany Sárfehér as the sparkling-base story.
Describe the climate in three words: hottest, coldest, driest, and frost as the hazard.
Know the labels: Kunsági OEM, Duna-Tisza közi OFJ, pezsgő, félédes.
traps: Kunság is sand, not loess; Szekszárd's loess hills lie west of the Danube, outside the district.
Ungrafted does not mean old or fine; most of the plain's own-rooted vines are young and make simple wine.
Cserszegi Fűszeres is a crossing, not a Muscat, though it smells like one; Irsai Olivér and Traminer are its parents.
Duna is the wine region, Duna-Tisza közi is the PGI, Kunság is the district; three names, three levels.
The atlas locator is one dot for a district that spans half the plain; its boundary is not a point.
The old course note's light wines on ungrafted vines is right, and phylloxera's dislike of quartz sand is the reason.

cards.f: Kunság: where, and what makes it unusual
cards.b: The sandy plain between the Danube and the Tisza, Hungary's largest district; quartz sand keeps phylloxera out, so vines grow on their own roots.

cards.f: Kunság's climate in a line
cards.b: The most continental in Hungary: hottest summers, coldest winters, most sunshine, least rain, and frost on the flat land as the constant hazard.

cards.f: The plain's three leading whites
cards.b: Cserszegi Fűszeres, Irsai Olivér and Olaszrizling; the first two are crossings bred for the sand, the third is Welschriesling.

cards.f: Cserszegi Fűszeres: parents and year
cards.b: Irsai Olivér crossed with Traminer, bred at Cserszegtomaj in 1960; spicy, Muscat-scented, early-drinking.

cards.f: Izsák's claim to fame
cards.b: Arany Sárfehér, the neutral high-acid white that bases Hungarian sparkling wine; Izsáki Arany Sárfehér is a protected name of its own.

cards.f: The wine region that holds Kunság, and its neighbours
cards.b: Duna, with Hajós-Baja and Csongrád; Duna-Tisza közi is the PGI the plain's volume wine carries.

cards.f: Kunság's reds in brief
cards.b: Kékfrankos, Kadarka and Zweigelt, light and soft on sand, mostly for young reds and rosé; old-vine Kadarka is the exception worth seeking.

cards.f: Why vineyards moved to the plain
cards.b: Phylloxera ruined the hill vineyards from the 1880s; the louse cannot tunnel through quartz sand, so the plain was planted ungrafted and in quantity.

questions.q: Why can vines on the plain between the Danube and the Tisza be planted on their own roots?
opts: Winter cold kills the louse each year
The vines are a resistant native species
questions.exp: Phylloxera needs a soil it can move through, and sand with a high quartz content defeats it. The louse survives cold winters elsewhere, and European vines are not resistant by nature.

questions.q: Hungary groups its districts into six wine regions. Which one holds Kunság?
questions.exp: Duna, the Danube region, takes in Kunság with Hajós-Baja and Csongrád. Pannon is the southern Transdanubian hill country, Balaton the lake districts and Somló.

questions.q: Under which protected geographical indication does most of the plain's volume wine leave Kunság?
questions.exp: Duna-Tisza közi, between the Danube and the Tisza, is the OFJ of the plain, with more varieties and higher yields than the Kunsági OEM. Dunántúli covers Transdanubia, Balatonmelléki the lake country and Felső-Magyarországi the north-east.

questions.q: Which two rivers bound the Kunság district on its western and eastern sides?
questions.exp: The district fills the sandy ridge between the Danube on the west and the Tisza on the east, above both rivers' flood plains. The Drava is the southern border with Croatia, the Hernád joins the Tisza from the north-east, and the Rába and Marcal flow in the west near Somló.

questions.q: One aromatic crossing of Irsai Olivér and Traminer, bred in 1960, leads the plain's whites. Name it.
questions.exp: Bred at Cserszegtomaj near Keszthely for frost resistance and aroma, it smells of Muscat and spice and is the sand's best-known glass. Irsai Olivér is itself a crossing.

questions.q: What soil dominates the vineyards of Kunság?
questions.exp: Wind-blown quartz sand over river alluvium, poor and fast-draining, is the plain's ground; loess is Szekszárd's, basalt Somló's and Badacsony's, limestone Villány's.

questions.q: A Hungarian label on a bottle of Izsák fizz reads pezsgő. What does the word mean?
questions.exp: Pezsgő is the Hungarian word for sparkling wine of any method; most of the plain's is tank-method from the neutral, high-acid Arany Sárfehér grown around Izsák.

questions.q: Which grape, neutral and high in acid, is the traditional base for the sparkling wines of the plain?
questions.exp: Arany Sárfehér's neutrality and acid make it the sparkling base, and Izsák's protected name rests on it. Cserszegi and Irsai are too aromatic; Kövidinka is a soft old variety for still wine.
